title: No "I have attained" (section 9)
hookLine: a stream-enterer does not think "I have entered the stream"; Subhuti rests in peace without that thought
tomorrow: A mind that rests on nothing (section 10)

lines: THE GUEST WHO SAYS HE'S HUMBLE.
THE SAME QUESTION AT EVERY STEP.
cards: At some dinner parties there's a guest who mentions, more than once, how little he cares about status. The more he says it, the less it sounds true.
Section nine of the Diamond Sutra is about the quiet opposite of that guest.
The Buddha walks Subhuti down the stages of the path, and at every step he asks the same thing: does someone who has reached this stage think, I have reached it?
At the end, Subhuti answers for himself, and he's the one the Buddha has praised.

teach.b: First, the stages. Early Buddhist teaching names them: the stream-enterer, who has entered the current that leads to awakening; the once-returner; the non-returner; and the arhat, the worthy one, fully freed.
Does a stream-enterer think, I have entered the stream?
No, Subhuti says, and the reason is the sutra's own kind of reason. A stream-enterer enters nothing: not sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches or things of the mind.
That's exactly why the name stream-enterer can be used. The same question comes at each stage, and the same answer.
An arhat who thought, I am an arhat, would be holding on to a self, a person, a being, a life, the very things the path lets go of. Third, Subhuti on himself.

The Buddha has praised him, he says, as one who dwells in peace, free of craving. But I don't think, I am an arhat free of craving. If I did, the Buddha wouldn't have said that Subhuti delights in peaceful dwelling.
The peace and the thought can't sit in the same chair.
The sutra isn't against reaching anything, or against doing good; it names every stage. What it drops is the credit line written afterward, the small voice that says, look what I did.
You carry a neighbor's groceries, and a minute later the narrator arrives to sign it. The groceries were carried either way.

how: In Buddhist communities, people are encouraged to do good quietly and to dedicate the merit to others rather than claim it; teachers use this section to warn against pride in one's own progress.

o: refusing ever to reach any stage of the path at all
keeping quiet about it so others won't feel jealous
reaching a stage without the thought, I have reached it

p: has entered the current to awakening
no sight, sound, smell, taste or touch
dwells in peace without the thought

s: Subhuti says he thinks of himself as free of craving
he says he doesn't think that, and that's why the Buddha can praise him for dwelling in peace.
in the sutra, a stream-enterer does not think 'I have entered the stream'
a stream-enterer enters nothing: not sights, sounds or any object of the senses.
section nine says the stages of the path are unreal and should be skipped
it names every stage. it drops the thought 'I have reached it'.

games.q: you're Subhuti. the Buddha has praised you for dwelling in peace. he asks whether you think, 'I am an arhat, free of craving.' what do you say?
o: yes: the Buddha said so himself.
no: if I thought that, he couldn't have praised me.
I'm not sure yet; ask me again later.
games.why: Subhuti says he doesn't think it. if he did, the Buddha wouldn't have said Subhuti delights in peaceful dwelling.

practice: Start with this sit itself: if a little narrator shows up, I'm doing well at this, I'm calmer than yesterday, don't scold it. Just say it again with the I taken out: sitting, breathing, calm for now.
Then let even those words fade, and stay with the breath.

wordCard.voice: No "I have attained." The one who has entered the stream doesn't think, I have entered it; Subhuti dwells in peace without that thought. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: one who has entered the stream; in Pali, sotapanna.

carryVoice: Your line: without "I did." Subhuti's peace has no signature on it. Back tomorrow with section ten.
